An eighteen-year-old schoolboy said of this:
“This is supposed to be a nihilist—a man as completely convinced of, and coated in, himself as E.[rnst] J.[ünger]?”
I have read Jünger’s two letters of 10 and 16 January 1950 closely.
“If, however, you had followed my advice and my example in the matter, you might no longer be alive today, but you would have the right to pass final judgment on me.”
I understand, and I fall silent.
So speaks one survivor to another!
He constructs two unreal conditional sentences. He says:

The survivor is wrong, because perhaps I would no longer be alive. But before that he says that he himself—although, after all, he too survived—would certainly no longer be alive, physically or psychologically, if he had followed me.
Is this not the sophistry of an ego-mad man who always has to be right?
An aftereffect of his mescaline experiment?
La guerre sainte, la guerre à la fois diabolique et divine.
Holy war: war that is at once diabolical and divine.
Ch. Journet, L’Église du Verbe Incarné, 1943, p. 360 ff.
They made pilgrimage to Jerusalem bearing arms. He relies on Carl Erdmann, The Origin of the Idea of Crusade, Stuttgart 1935.
Within the problematic concept of “holy war,” J.[ournet] makes a distinction in discussing the Crusades between “the canonical power of the clergy and their non-canonical powers”!
“It will then become clear that ‘holy wars’ are bound to the existence, or the surviving remnants, of a Christendom of the sacral type.”
War, like death, comes from sin:
In the Responsa of Nicholas I to the Bulgarians (866), we read:
“The struggles of wars and battles, and likewise the beginnings of every quarrel, were certainly devised by the deceitful art of the devil.”
War is permissible only in an emergency.
Nevertheless, Joseph de Maistre is not entirely wrong to call war “divine” in the seventh dialogue of the Soirées de Saint-Pétersbourg, because war cannot be explained in purely human terms:
“There is no way to explain how war is humanly possible.”
J. de M.: therefore divine punishment; divine in the sense in which hell is divine. The Deus indignatus—the indignant God—imposes it.
At the beginning of war there is always sin. But war is just when it is occasioned, not inspired—so he says, p. 363.
But is the idea of a just war not even sadder?
St. Augustine asks this in De Civitate Dei 19, chapter 7.
(This chapter 7 is magnificent and more important than most books about just war; chapter 8 as well, including the distinction between friend and enemy!)
Then Thomas, Summa Theologiae II–II, question 40, articles 1 and 3.
“After reading this description of the just war,” Journet says, “one naturally asks how many wars have ever been completely just. I think one could count them on the fingers of one hand.”
Here a new and devastating concept appears: the one-hundred-percent just war!
J.[ournet] refers to Gustave Thibon, Études carmélitaines, 1939, pp. 63–67:
War is just only when the Christian faces a choice “between war and the denial of his essence as a human being.”
Do these good and righteous people really not see that this turns war into a war of annihilation?!
Here the Christian must be careful not to become the victim of deception—“and this will not be easy, and only saints will be fully capable of it!!”
G. Thibon, with Journet agreeing, p. 364 note.
The Christian must realize the “paradox”: inwardly, love and the renunciation of every judgment— “Christian justice, which judges no one!!”
In the end, only saints can do it.
The Cluniac reformers spread the idea of Christian knighthood. They “transfigured” the Germanic idea of combat.
The distinction between just wars and holy wars appears on p. 365.
A just war does not become holy merely because the pope recognizes the justice of its cause.
Collaboration, approval, consecration—none of these is enough if the cause concerns secular interests.
Nor, even in a sacral regime, is it enough merely that one is dealing with a crime such as heresy.
Admittedly, wars encouraged and approved by the Church in defense of the faith could be called just wars.
“But we prefer to reserve this name, if the name must be used at all (!), for wars for which the pope himself assumes responsibility and which we shall now discuss.”
Answer, following H. Pissard, La guerre sainte en pays chrétien, Paris 1912:
“Holy wars are just wars (!) which the Church not only encourages but also rewards with its spiritual favors.”
But, Journet says, we do not claim that they are undertaken or directed by the Church. That is, they do not arise from canonical power.
“They are undertaken and directed by the pope’s extra-canonical power, acting either as head of the Papal State or as guardian of Christendom.”
The pure holy war—that is, a war waged by the pope on the basis of canonical powers—is, according to Journet, impossible. It has also never occurred.
Not even against the Albigensians in 1208–14.

As an honest man, he argues that war was simply the logical escalation of the interdict, the release of vassals from their obligations, and their “exposure as prey,” undertaken in order to execute canonical judgments against heretics who had become too powerful, when the suzerain—not the sovereign!—could not or would not lend the support of his sword.
“The Church as such does not wage war.”
Disgusting, this comme tel—“as such.” It reminds one far too much of:
“The Party as such stands on the foundation of positive Christianity.”
Carl Erdmann claims that Augustine raised the suppression of the Donatists by Emperor Honorius to the level of holy war.
The author of this war was God himself, and the soldiers were God’s ministri—his servants.
But Augustine always protests against heretics being punished with death. He fears that the blood of the heretics will fall back upon the Church!!
